catalog_quote: Nahavaq does not have lexical stress. I also find no convincing evidence of fixed word-stress. It seems that any prominence that exists can be explained by segmental phonology and/or prosody at a level higher than the word. ... I often perceive penultimate stress on Nahavaq words spoken in isolation. ... There are however, Nahavaq words that I hear as having other stress patterns. For example, when the penultimate syllable contains a higher vowel than the final syllable, I often hear prominence on the final syllable ... I also often hear syllables that have a glottal onset as prominent ... However, when I listen to recordings of Nahavaq words in isolation, I frequently change my mind about which syllable sounds most prominent. ... even with training speakers could not confidently or consistently identify any one syllable as any stronger than others in the word. ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all quoted fragments and the domain quote found verbatim at the stated pages (46-48) of the Dimock 2009 PDF we hold/text. (2) Deciding source is a 2009 300-page reference grammar (PhD, VUW) with a dedicated stress section that combines perception tests with instrumental measurements; Glottolog and Crossref show no competing grammar, phonology article or instrumental study for Nahavaq, and the author's COOL7 2007 talk on the same data was never published. (3) Nothing worth wish-listing: the only candidate (the unpublished COOL7 presentation) is subsumed by the thesis section we hold; older Malakula sources (Deacon 1934, Charpentier 1982, survey wordlists) do not describe stress. (4) Coding 'no-word-stress' with the paraphrase attributing perceived penultimate prominence to utterance-final intonation matches the source exactly (pp. 46-50, and 2.6 p. 50 'gradual fall in pitch
